topic.subject: science
topic.title: Force and laws of motion
topic.scope: inertia, balanced and unbalanced forces, Newton's three laws, momentum, action-reaction pairs

misconceptions.statement: An object in motion must have a force acting on it to keep moving.
misconceptions.why: Everyday experience shows that objects like toys or bicycles stop moving if we stop pushing them.
misconceptions.fix: An object will continue to move at a constant speed in a straight line unless an unbalanced force acts on it to change its state.

probe.question: A hockey puck slides across a frictionless ice rink. What force is needed to keep it moving at a constant speed?
probe.wrong_answer: A constant forward force is needed to overcome the motion.

misconceptions.statement: If an object is not moving, there are no forces acting on it.
misconceptions.why: Students often confuse 'no motion' with 'no forces' because they equate force only with visible movement.
misconceptions.fix: An object at rest can have multiple forces acting on it, but they are balanced, resulting in a net force of zero.

probe.question: A book is lying still on a table. Are there any forces acting on it?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because the book is not moving.

misconceptions.statement: Heavier objects have more inertia because they are harder to lift.
misconceptions.why: Students conflate the everyday meaning of 'heavy' (weight) with the scientific definition of inertia (resistance to change in motion).
misconceptions.fix: Inertia is the inherent property of an object to resist changes in its state of motion, which is directly proportional to its mass, not its weight.

probe.question: Which has more inertia: a 1kg ball on Earth or a 1kg ball in deep space?
probe.wrong_answer: The one on Earth because it is heavier.

misconceptions.statement: Force is the same thing as acceleration.
misconceptions.why: Students often see that pushing harder (more force) makes something go faster (more acceleration) and fail to distinguish the cause from the effect.
misconceptions.fix: Force is the cause of the change in motion, while acceleration is the resulting rate of change of velocity.

probe.question: If an object is moving at a constant velocity, how much force is acting on it?
probe.wrong_answer: It must have a constant force acting on it to keep the acceleration going.

misconceptions.statement: Action-reaction forces cancel each other out so nothing can ever move.
misconceptions.why: Students misapply the concept of balanced forces (which act on the same object) to action-reaction pairs (which act on different objects).
misconceptions.fix: Action and reaction forces act on different objects, so they never cancel each other out; they cause different objects to accelerate.

probe.question: A horse pulls a cart. If the cart pulls back on the horse with an equal force, why does the cart move forward?
probe.wrong_answer: The cart shouldn't move because the forces are equal and opposite, so they cancel out.
